resources.string: Animal Diversity Web · University of Michigan
Smithsonian National Zoo
San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance
National Park Service
Lion
A powerful social cat whose pride brings together related females, their young and resident males.
African savannas, grasslands and dry scrub; a separate population inhabits the Gir region of India.
Large herbivores including zebra and wildebeest. It also scavenges and takes smaller prey when available.
Females often hunt together and nurse cubs. Roars and scent marks advertise the territory.
Golden coat, rounded ears and a tail ending in a dark tuft. Adult males usually have a conspicuous mane.
Tiger
A large Asian cat adapted to stalking and ambushing prey under cover.
Forests, grasslands and mangroves with cover, water and sufficient prey; it tolerates very different climates.
Mostly ungulates, including deer and wild pigs. Powerful forelimbs help subdue prey.
Usually solitary except mothers with cubs. It marks its range with scent and is a capable swimmer.
Orange coat with dark vertical stripes, pale belly and ringed tail. Each stripe pattern differs.
Leopard
An agile African and Asian cat whose spotted coat breaks up its outline in vegetation.
Rainforests, savannas, rocky country and mountains; shelter is important for resting and stalking.
An opportunistic carnivore taking antelope, monkeys, rodents, birds and other available animals.
Often rests in trees and can haul carcasses into branches, beyond the reach of some competitors.
Long tail and rosettes generally without central dots. A black coat can still conceal visible rosettes.
Jaguar
A robust American cat with powerful jaws and a close association with water.
Dense tropical forests, wetlands and river margins; it also uses scrub and woodland.
Deer, peccaries and many other vertebrates, including turtles and caimans. It ambushes prey from concealment.
Mainly solitary. It swims well and may seek shade beside water during hot periods.
Stocky body, broad head and rosettes often enclosing small dark spots; some individuals are black.
Cheetah
A slender cat specialised for brief, rapid pursuit rather than prolonged running.
Open grasslands and dry landscapes with room to pursue prey and places to conceal young.
Gazelles and other small or medium ungulates; hares and birds are also taken.
Males may form coalitions. A high-speed chase is followed by rest to recover from the exertion.
Long legs, small head, round black spots and dark tear marks from eyes to muzzle.
Puma
A widely distributed American cat, also known as the cougar or mountain lion.
Forests, mountains, brush and grasslands with prey and cover; caves and rock crevices provide shelter.
Mostly deer and other ungulates, supplemented by smaller mammals and birds.
Solitary adults mark their ranges. They conceal large kills under debris and return to feed.
Plain tawny or grey-brown coat, small rounded ears and a long dark-tipped tail; cubs are spotted.
Canada lynx
A northern forest cat whose broad furry paws help support its weight on snow.
Boreal forests and dense undergrowth in North America; it also enters more open or rocky areas.
Snowshoe hares are especially important; rodents and birds supplement its diet.
Usually solitary, it stalks or waits in ambush. Population fluctuations can follow those of its principal prey.
Ear tufts, cheek ruff, very short dark-tipped tail and disproportionately broad paws.
Domestic cat
A domesticated felid retaining the senses and hunting movements of a small predator.
Human homes and settlements; free-ranging populations occupy nearby urban and rural habitats.
A carnivore requiring animal-derived nutrients. Free-ranging cats take small mammals, birds and other prey.
Scent rubbing and scratching communicate identity. Social tolerance varies with resources and individual history.
Flexible body, retractile claws and sensitive whiskers. Coat, size and tail vary among breeds.
Grey wolf
A social canid whose family groups cooperate in travelling, hunting and raising pups.
Forests, tundra, mountains and grasslands across parts of the Northern Hemisphere.
Often ungulates such as deer, supplemented by smaller mammals and carrion according to local availability.
Packs communicate with howls, body posture and scent marks. Pups are cared for within the group.
Long legs, broad muzzle, erect ears and bushy tail; fur ranges from pale to almost black.
Red fox
An adaptable small canid that succeeds in both natural and human-modified environments.
Woodland edges, farmland, grasslands and towns; sheltered dens are used for rearing cubs.
Rodents, rabbits, insects and fruit; its opportunistic diet changes with the season.
Frequently active at dusk and night. It caches food and uses scent to mark familiar routes.
Pointed muzzle and ears, dark lower legs and a long bushy tail often tipped white.
Arctic fox
A compact Arctic canid with dense fur and furry foot soles that reduce heat loss.
Arctic tundra and coastal environments; underground dens shelter breeding families.
Lemmings and other small mammals, birds, eggs and carrion; coastal populations use marine resources.
Food can be stored near dens. It travels extensively when food becomes scarce.
Short rounded ears, short muzzle and thick tail; white and darker blue colour forms occur.
Brown bear
A large omnivorous bear whose diet and activity vary strongly with local conditions.
Forests, mountains, tundra margins and open country offering food and secure resting sites.
Plant shoots, berries and roots, insects, carrion and vertebrate prey; some populations exploit salmon runs.
Usually solitary except mothers with young. In seasonal climates it spends winter in a den.
Prominent shoulder hump, rounded ears and long foreclaws; coat colour varies considerably.
Polar bear
A marine-associated bear adapted to hunting on sea ice and swimming between ice floes.
Arctic sea ice and nearby coasts; ice provides access to its principal prey.
Mainly seals, particularly ringed seals; carcasses and other animal foods are also used.
Often hunts at seal breathing holes. Pregnant females use maternity dens for sheltering cubs.
Pale dense coat, elongated neck, small ears and broad paws; dark skin lies beneath the fur.
Giant panda
A bear whose feeding anatomy and daily routine are strongly specialised around bamboo.
Mountain forests of China with a bamboo understorey and suitable shelter.
Mostly bamboo leaves, stems and shoots. A modified wrist bone helps grasp stems while feeding.
Usually solitary; scent marks and vocal signals communicate between individuals.
White face and trunk with dark ears, eye patches, shoulders and legs.
African savanna elephant
A large terrestrial herbivore whose trunk combines breathing, smelling and grasping functions.
African savannas, woodland and grassland, with movement between food and water resources.
Grasses, leaves, bark and branches. Feeding and movement can reshape the vegetation.
Females and young form family groups; adult males often travel apart. Touch, calls and scent support communication.
Large fan-shaped ears, long trunk and usually tusks in both sexes; the back is often concave.
Asian elephant
An Asian elephant with a highly dexterous trunk used to gather food and investigate its surroundings.
Forests, grasslands and scrub of southern and southeastern Asia, with access to water.
Grasses, leaves, woody plants, bark and fruit; the trunk collects and places food in the mouth.
Family groups centre on females and their young. Adult males may live alone or in loose associations.
Smaller ears than the African savanna elephant, domed forehead and a single finger-like trunk tip.
Black rhinoceros
A browsing rhinoceros whose flexible upper lip selects leaves and twigs.
African savannas, thorn scrub and woodland, usually within reach of drinking water.
Leaves, shoots and woody twigs rather than mainly short grasses.
Adults are often solitary. They use dung, urine and scent to communicate along familiar paths.
Two horns and a pointed, prehensile upper lip; a robust body with relatively short legs.
Greater one-horned rhinoceros
An Asian rhinoceros with conspicuous folded skin and a single nasal horn.
Floodplain grasslands, river margins and adjoining woodland in the Indian subcontinent.
Mostly grasses, with leaves, aquatic plants and fruit also eaten.
It frequently wallows and bathes. Adults are usually solitary but may gather at feeding or bathing sites.
One horn, thick skin folds resembling armour and raised bumps on shoulders and limbs.
Hippopotamus
A large semi-aquatic mammal that rests in water and mainly feeds on land.
Rivers, lakes and pools in sub-Saharan Africa with nearby grassland for grazing.
Mainly grasses cropped with broad muscular lips during night-time grazing excursions.
Groups rest together in water; males defend access to parts of the water habitat. It returns from grazing before dawn.
Barrel-shaped body, broad mouth, short legs and eyes, ears and nostrils set high on the head.
American bison
A North American grassland herbivore that shapes vegetation through grazing and wallowing.
Prairies and open country of North America; surviving wild herds use protected grassland landscapes.
Grasses and sedges form the bulk of its diet, with feeding varying by season.
Lives in herds; bulls compete during the rut. Wallowing leaves shallow depressions in the ground.
Massive shoulder hump, shaggy forequarters, smaller hindquarters and short curved horns.
Red deer
A large ruminant deer whose males grow and shed branched antlers each year.
Woodland, forest edges and open uplands, with cover and varied plant resources.
Grasses, herbs, leaves and woody shoots; rumination helps process plant material.
Males compete and vocalise during the rut; females and young often form groups.
Reddish-brown summer coat, paler rump and short tail; adult males carry branching antlers.
Moose
A tall northern deer adapted to browsing shrubs and moving through wet ground.
Boreal and temperate forests, especially wet areas, young woodland and lake margins.
Leaves and shoots in summer, woody twigs in winter; aquatic plants are also consumed.
Usually less social than other deer. It swims well and often feeds around dawn and dusk.
Long legs, drooping muzzle and a throat bell; males often have broad palmate antlers.
Domestic cattle
A domesticated ruminant whose multi-chambered stomach supports the digestion of coarse vegetation.
Pastures, rangelands and farm environments worldwide, managed by people.
Grasses and other plant material. Microbes in the rumen break down food before it is rechewed.
Herds have social relationships and a dominance order. Mothers recognise and protect calves.
Sturdy body, cloven hooves and a tufted tail. Horn presence and coat pattern depend on breed.
Wild boar
An adaptable omnivore that searches soil and litter using its strong snout.
Woodland, scrub, farmland and wetlands providing cover, food and water.
Roots, nuts, fruit and other plant foods, with worms, insects, eggs and carrion.
Females and young form groups; mature males are often solitary. Wallowing helps cooling and skin care.
Coarse bristles, long snout and visible canines in mature animals; young have pale longitudinal stripes.
Domestic horse
A grazing equid with long legs and a single weight-bearing toe on each foot.
Managed pasture and farm environments; free-ranging populations occupy open grassland and scrub.
Primarily grasses and other fibrous plants. Domestic feeding depends on management and work.
Social groups develop dominance relationships. Body posture, ears and vocalisations convey signals.
Long head and neck, mane, long-haired tail and a solid hoof on each foot; coat varies by breed.
Chimpanzee
A great ape with flexible social relationships and learned feeding traditions.
African tropical forests, woodland–savanna mosaics and mountain forests.
Fruit, leaves, seeds and insects; some communities hunt other mammals or use tools to obtain food.
Communities split into smaller parties and reunite. Individuals groom each other and build sleeping nests.
Long arms, short legs, no tail and dark body hair; the face is largely bare.
Bonobo
A great ape closely related to chimpanzees, with important female social bonds.
Tropical forest in the Congo Basin, south of the Congo River; secondary forest is also used.
Mostly fruit, supplemented by leaves, shoots, seeds and animal foods.
Groups repeatedly divide and merge as food availability changes. Mothers can influence the social position of sons.
Dark face, long dark hair often parted on the head, relatively slender limbs and no tail.
Western gorilla
A powerful forest ape living in social groups that often include a dominant adult male.
Tropical forests of western equatorial Africa, including secondary woodland.
Fruit, leaves, stems and other plant material; diet varies with the available vegetation.
Groups travel and feed together. Chest beating is a display; nests are built for rest.
Broad chest, long arms, bare dark face and no tail; mature males develop a silver-grey back.
Senegal galago
A small nocturnal primate whose powerful hind legs permit long leaps between branches.
Savanna woodland and bushy habitats south of the Sahara.
Insects, fruit and tree gums provide food; sensitive hearing helps locate prey.
Forages at night and shelters during the day. Flexible ears can be folded back.
Very large eyes, large thin ears, long tail and grey-brown woolly fur.
House mouse
A small rodent that has spread widely through its association with people.
Buildings, barns and stores of food, but also fields and sheltered outdoor sites.
Seeds and other plant foods, with insects and a variety of human food when available.
Usually nocturnal; it makes sheltered nests and uses odours to recognise individuals and territories.
Small body, pointed snout, rounded ears and a long sparsely haired tail.
Black rat
An agile climbing rodent historically spread by ships and trade.
Buildings, farms and wooded areas, often nesting above ground in roofs or trees.
Fruit, grain and other plants, with insects and additional animal food when available.
Often lives in social groups with dominance relationships. Its climbing ability helps it exploit high refuges.
Relatively large ears, pointed muzzle and a tail usually longer than head and body; colour is variable.
Red squirrel
An arboreal rodent adept at moving through branches and opening hard seeds.
Mature coniferous, deciduous and mixed forests with trees suitable for nesting.
Tree seeds and nuts; fungi, buds and other foods supplement seasonal supplies.
Active by day, it buries food and builds nests. It does not hibernate, but reduces activity in poor weather.
Bushy balancing tail, pale underside and ear tufts especially in winter; back colour ranges from red to dark brown.
American beaver
A semi-aquatic rodent whose building activity can create wetland habitat.
North American streams, rivers, ponds and lakes with woody plants along their banks.
Bark and the growing layer beneath it, twigs, buds and aquatic vegetation.
Family groups maintain lodges and sometimes dams. A tail slap on water warns of disturbance.
Broad flat scaly tail, large orange incisors, dense waterproof fur and webbed hind feet.
European hedgehog
A small ground-dwelling mammal whose modified hairs form protective spines.
Hedgerows, woodland margins, grassland and gardens with nesting cover.
Mostly invertebrates, including beetles and other insects; additional foods are taken opportunistically.
Generally solitary and nocturnal. It rolls into a spiny ball when threatened and hibernates in cold seasons.
Rounded spiny back, hairy underside, short legs and a long pointed snout.
European rabbit
A social burrowing lagomorph; it is the ancestor of domestic rabbits.
Open scrub, grassland and farmland with soft soil for burrows and nearby cover.
Grasses, leaves, buds and bark. Reingesting soft droppings recovers nutrients from plant digestion.
Colonies may share complex warrens. Social rank influences access to shelter and reproduction.
Long ears, strong hind legs and a short tail with a pale underside; wild coats are usually grey-brown.
European hare
A long-legged lagomorph that relies on concealment and rapid escape rather than a warren.
Open farmland, fields and pastures with hedges or small patches of woodland.
Grasses, herbs and crops; woody material may be eaten when green food is scarce.
Rests in a shallow depression called a form. Young are born furred and more developed than rabbit kits.
Very long black-tipped ears, long hind legs and brown mottled fur that does not turn white in winter.
Large flying fox
A fruit bat with a fox-like face that helps disperse seeds and transport pollen.
Tropical forests and mangroves of Southeast Asia; large trees provide daytime roosts.
Fruit, nectar and flowers; teeth and tongue extract juices and soft plant material.
Leaves communal tree roosts around sunset to forage, then returns to rest hanging upside down.
Fox-like muzzle, pointed ears, dark fur and broad membranous wings.
Greater mouse-eared bat
A European insectivorous bat that often captures prey on the ground.
Open woodland for feeding; caves and buildings provide roosts and seasonal shelters.
Mainly ground beetles, with other large insects such as moths also consumed.
Nocturnal and often colonial. Seasonal movements link summer roosts with winter hibernation sites.
Relatively large ears, brownish upper fur, paler underside and broad membranous wings.
Red kangaroo
A large Australian marsupial whose young continue development attached to a teat inside the pouch.
Dry inland grasslands, open plains and scrub with scattered shade and shelter.
Grasses and other low plants; it selects feeding sites according to available forage.
Moves by hopping with powerful hind limbs. The muscular tail balances jumps and supports resting postures.
Large hind feet, small forelimbs, long heavy tail and erect ears; males are usually more reddish than females.
Koala
A tree-dwelling marsupial with a specialised leaf diet and a low-energy daily routine.
Eucalypt woodland and forest in eastern Australia, where suitable food trees occur.
Mostly leaves from selected eucalyptus species; its digestive system processes fibrous food.
Spends much time resting in branches. Males use loud calls and scent during breeding interactions.
Large furry rounded ears, broad dark nose, grey fur and no conspicuous external tail.
Platypus
An egg-laying mammal whose sensitive bill helps detect underwater prey.
Rivers, streams and lagoons of eastern Australia and Tasmania; banks hold burrows.
Aquatic invertebrates collected while diving; small animal foods vary with local availability.
Usually solitary, it forages in water and rests in bank burrows. Males possess venom-bearing hind-leg spurs.
Broad flat bill, dense brown fur, webbed feet and a flattened tail.
Harbour seal
A coastal seal adapted to underwater pursuit and regular resting ashore.
Temperate and cold northern coasts, estuaries, bays and rocky or sandy haul-out sites.
Mainly fish, with squid, octopus and crustaceans also taken according to local abundance.
Often rests with other seals but lacks a strongly organised group. Hauling out supports rest, moulting and nursing.
Rounded head without external ear flaps, spotted coat and short flippers; nostrils close in water.
Common bottlenose dolphin
A toothed cetacean using echolocation and social coordination while feeding.
Warm and temperate coastal and offshore seas; coastal and oceanic populations differ in habitat use.
Fish, squid and crustaceans, located using sound and taken with varied local hunting techniques.
Groups often split and reform. Social interactions include play, gentle contact and cooperative movements.
Grey body, short distinct beak, curved dorsal fin and horizontal tail flukes.
Orca
A large oceanic dolphin whose hunting traditions differ among populations.
Marine waters worldwide, from coastal seas to offshore environments.
Fish or marine mammals and other prey, depending on population; diets should not be assumed identical.
Strong social bonds link family groups. Calls and coordinated movements support hunting and travel.
Black back, white underside and white eye patch; a tall dorsal fin, especially in adult males.
Blue whale
A vast baleen whale that filters small crustaceans from water instead of using teeth.
Oceans worldwide; feeding and breeding areas may be linked by seasonal migration.
Predominantly krill, engulfed with water and retained by baleen as water leaves the mouth.
Often alone or in pairs. Low-frequency sounds help communicate over large distances.
Long blue-grey mottled body, small dorsal fin set far back and throat grooves.
Humpback whale
A baleen whale with exceptionally long pectoral flippers and elaborate vocal displays.
Coastal and offshore seas; many populations migrate between cooler feeding areas and warmer breeding waters.
Krill and schooling fish, engulfed in large mouthfuls and filtered through baleen.
Breaches and tail slaps occur; males produce long songs, especially on breeding grounds.
Very long flippers, knobbly head and throat grooves; the tail underside has individual patterns.
Dugong
A marine herbivore whose grazing leaves feeding trails through seagrass beds.
Sheltered coastal waters of the Indo-Pacific with suitable seagrass beds.
Seagrass leaves and underground plant parts gathered with a muscular downward-facing mouth.
Often seen singly or as mother–calf pairs; movements follow the availability of seagrass.
Rounded grey body, paddle-like foreflippers, downturned muzzle and a fluked tail rather than a round paddle.
Beech marten
An agile omnivorous mustelid that often lives close to human settlements.
Open woodland, rocky ground and settlements; buildings may provide sheltered dens.
Small mammals, birds, eggs and insects, with fruit and berries important in some seasons.
Mostly solitary and nocturnal. A capable climber, it marks its range with scent and may cache surplus food.
Brown or grey-brown fur, bushy tail and usually a pale throat bib extending onto the chest.
European pine marten
A climbing forest mustelid whose long tail supports balance among branches.
Deciduous, mixed and coniferous forests, with cavities, old nests or rock crevices for resting.
Small mammals, birds and insects, with fruit and berries contributing seasonally.
Often active at dusk and night. It hunts in trees and on the forest floor and stores some food.
Rich brown fur, bushy tail, prominent rounded ears and a creamy to yellowish throat patch.
Wolverine
A strong northern mustelid that combines scavenging with hunting across large ranges.
Boreal forests, tundra and cold mountains with relatively undisturbed terrain.
Carrion and mammalian prey, with smaller animals taken when available; food may be cached.
Usually solitary and active throughout the year. Cold conditions help preserve stored animal food.
Broad head, rounded ears, powerful short legs and dark fur with lighter side bands.
Common ostrich
A flightless African bird specialised for running on powerful long legs.
Open savanna, grassland and dry country with good visibility.
Mostly plant foods such as leaves and seeds, with insects and other small items.
Runs to escape threats; eggs may be laid in communal nests and adults guard the brood.
Very long bare neck and legs, small head and two toes per foot; adult males are black and white.
Emperor penguin
A flightless marine bird that breeds on Antarctic sea ice during the cold season.
Antarctic sea ice for breeding and nearby ocean waters for feeding.
Fish, squid and crustaceans captured during deep underwater dives.
The male incubates an egg on his feet beneath a skin fold; adults huddle to conserve heat.
Black head and back, pale belly, yellow-orange neck patches and stiff flipper-like wings.
Red junglefowl
A ground-foraging Asian bird from which domestic chickens descend.
Forest, scrub and forest edges of tropical Asia, often near clearings.
Seeds, fruit, green plant material and small invertebrates uncovered by scratching.
Social groups forage on the ground but roost above it. Male calls and displays signal status.
Males have a red comb, bright hackles and long curved tail feathers; females are mottled brown.
Rock pigeon
A cliff-nesting pigeon whose domestic descendants commonly live in cities.
Natural cliffs and rocky ledges; buildings offer similar nesting sites to urban populations.
Mostly seeds and grain, with other available foods used around people.
Often feeds in flocks. Both parents produce crop milk to nourish newly hatched young.
Wild-type grey body, iridescent neck, two dark wing bars and dark tail band; domestic forms vary.
Mallard
A dabbling duck that gathers food at the surface or by tipping forward in shallow water.
Freshwater wetlands, ponds, lakes and rivers, including urban parks.
Seeds and aquatic plants, with insects and other invertebrates; diet changes with season and age.
Pairs form seasonally. The female nests and leads the ducklings, which feed for themselves.
Breeding male with green head and pale neck ring; female mottled brown. Both have a blue wing patch.
Mute swan
A large waterbird that reaches submerged plants using its long neck.
Lakes, slow rivers, ponds and sheltered coastal wetlands.
Mainly aquatic vegetation, with some small aquatic animals incidentally taken.
Pairs defend nesting areas. Adults lead the young and may vigorously repel intruders.
White adult plumage, curved neck and orange bill with a black basal knob; young are grey-brown.
Greylag goose
A social grazing goose that is an ancestor of many domestic goose breeds.
Wetlands, lakes and marshes with nearby grassland or farmland.
Grasses, shoots, roots and seeds; feeding frequently takes place on land.
Family groups remain together while feeding in flocks. Some populations migrate between seasonal sites.
Grey-brown plumage, pale belly, sturdy orange or pinkish bill and pale forewing.
Common raven
A large intelligent corvid with flexible feeding strategies and complex social signals.
Mountains, coasts, woodland and open landscapes; cliffs and tall trees provide nests.
Carrion, invertebrates, small vertebrates and plant foods; an opportunistic omnivore.
Pairs defend territories, while non-breeders may gather at food sources. Calls and aerial displays communicate.
Glossy black plumage, heavy bill, shaggy throat and wedge-shaped tail in flight.
Eurasian magpie
A conspicuous long-tailed corvid, comfortable in many human-modified landscapes.
Open woodland, farmland, hedges, parks and gardens with trees for nesting.
Insects, small animals, eggs, carrion and plant foods, according to opportunity.
Builds a large stick nest, often with a roof. Territorial pairs and larger non-breeding groups occur.
Black-and-white body, very long tail and blue-green metallic reflections on dark feathers.
House sparrow
A small social bird closely associated with human buildings and food sources.
Settlements, farms, gardens and urban spaces; cavities provide nest sites.
Seeds and grain dominate the adult diet; insects are especially important for nestlings.
Feeds and roosts in groups. Nesting pairs use cavities or sheltered structural gaps.
Stout conical bill; male with grey crown and dark bib, female with brown back and pale eyebrow.
European robin
A small territorial songbird frequently seen feeding close to the ground.
Woodland undergrowth, hedges and gardens with low cover and nest shelter.
Insects, worms and other invertebrates, supplemented by fruit in some seasons.
Singing and displays defend feeding or breeding areas. It may follow disturbed soil to catch exposed prey.
Orange-red face and breast bordered by grey, brown upperparts and pale belly; juveniles are mottled.
Common blackbird
A thrush that searches leaf litter and soil for food and sings from raised perches.
Woodland, parks, gardens and scrub with dense cover for nesting.
Worms and other invertebrates, plus berries and fruit when available.
Often feeds on the ground, pausing to look and listen. Males sing to advertise breeding territories.
Male black with yellow-orange bill and eye ring; female brown with a subtly mottled breast.
Great tit
A versatile woodland songbird that readily uses nest cavities and artificial boxes.
Woodland, hedges, orchards, parks and gardens.
Insects and larvae, particularly during breeding, with seeds and nuts in other seasons.
Pairs defend breeding sites. Outside breeding it may join mixed feeding flocks.
Black head with white cheeks, yellow belly crossed by a black stripe and greenish back.
Eurasian blue tit
A small agile tit that searches fine branches and leaves for hidden food.
Deciduous woodland, hedges and gardens with trees and nesting cavities.
Small insects and larvae, supplemented by seeds and other plant foods.
May hang upside down while feeding. Nest cavities hold broods tended by both parents.
Blue crown, wings and tail, white cheeks, dark eye stripe and yellow underside.
Common kingfisher
A waterside bird that dives from perches to capture small aquatic prey.
Rivers, streams, lakes and sheltered waters with suitable perches and nesting banks.
Mostly small fish, with aquatic insects and other small aquatic animals.
Watches the water from a perch, then plunges. A tunnel excavated in a bank contains the nest.
Blue-green upperparts, orange underside, large pointed bill and short tail.
Great spotted woodpecker
A climbing bird with a strong bill and stiff tail used while working on tree trunks.
Woodlands, parks and gardens with mature trees or suitable dead wood.
Insects and larvae from wood, plus seeds and nuts; feeding varies with season.
Excavates nest holes. Drumming communicates through repeated bill strikes on resonant surfaces.
Black-and-white plumage, white shoulder patches and red under the tail; males have red at the nape.
Barn owl
A nocturnal owl whose hearing helps locate prey even in poor light.
Open farmland and grassland near buildings, tree cavities or other sheltered nests.
Mostly small mammals, captured during low searching flights or from perches.
Usually hunts at night. Indigestible bones and fur are expelled as pellets.
Heart-shaped pale facial disc, dark eyes, buff upperparts and pale underparts.
Eurasian eagle-owl
A large owl equipped to take a wide range of vertebrate prey.
Rocky country, cliffs and woodland, with sheltered nesting or resting sites.
Mammals and birds, with prey selection depending on local abundance.
Mostly active at night and dusk. Territorial calls announce occupancy and support pair contact.
Large orange eyes, tall feather ear tufts and heavily patterned brown plumage.
Common kestrel
A small falcon known for hovering while searching the ground for prey.
Open farmland, grassland and cities with elevated nesting sites and hunting space.
Small mammals and insects, with birds or reptiles depending on local conditions.
Hovers or watches from a perch before dropping onto prey. Often uses ledges or old nests.
Rufous spotted back, pointed wings and long tail; adult male has grey head and tail.
Osprey
A fish-catching raptor with feet and talons adapted to gripping slippery prey.
Coasts, lakes and rivers with open water and tall nest supports.
Almost entirely fish, caught by plunging feet first into water.
Builds bulky stick nests and often returns to established nesting areas. Many populations migrate.
Brown upperparts, pale underside, dark eye stripe and long wings often held with a bend.
White stork
A long-legged bird that takes varied small prey while walking through open habitats.
Wet grassland, marshes and farmland with large nest sites on trees or structures.
Insects, amphibians, small mammals and other small animals depending on local availability.
Bill clattering is used in displays at the nest. Migrating birds exploit rising air to soar.
White body, black flight feathers, long red bill and long red legs.
Grey heron
A patient wading predator that strikes quickly with its long bill.
Rivers, lakes, wetlands and estuaries, often near trees suitable for colony nests.
Fish, amphibians and other small animals, sometimes including mammals on land.
Stands still or stalks slowly in shallow water. Often breeds in tree-nesting colonies.
Grey back, pale neck, dark head stripe and long yellowish bill; neck folded during flight.
Atlantic puffin
A compact seabird using its wings to propel itself underwater while fishing.
North Atlantic seas; breeding colonies use grassy cliff tops, islands and coastal slopes.
Small schooling fish gathered during dives and carried crosswise in the bill for chicks.
Breeds in burrows or crevices, then spends much of the non-breeding season at sea.
Black upperparts, white belly, pale cheeks and a deep colourful breeding bill.
Common tern
A slender seabird that plunge-dives to capture prey near the water surface.
Coasts, islands, lakes and river margins; nests on sparsely vegetated ground.
Mostly small fish, with aquatic invertebrates also taken.
Breeds in colonies and defends nests vigorously. Seasonal migrations connect distant waters.
Long narrow wings, forked tail and black breeding cap; breeding bill usually red with a dark tip.
Common cuckoo
A brood parasite whose females place eggs in the nests of other bird species.
Woodland edges, scrub, wetlands and open habitats where suitable host birds nest.
Insects, particularly caterpillars, including hairy caterpillars avoided by many birds.
Host parents incubate the egg and feed the young cuckoo. Males give the familiar repeated two-note call.
Slender body, long tail and pointed wings; adults often grey above with a finely barred pale belly.
Nile crocodile
A large African crocodilian that captures prey at the boundary between land and water.
Rivers, lakes and wetlands, with banks used for basking and nesting.
Young take insects and small animals; adults eat fish and larger vertebrates, and sometimes scavenge.
Often waits partly submerged before striking. Large prey may be torn apart by rotating in the water.
Armoured back, long muscular tail and relatively narrow snout; some lower teeth remain visible with the mouth closed.
American alligator
A freshwater crocodilian whose nesting and digging create refuges used by other wetland animals.
Swamps, marshes, rivers and lakes in the southeastern United States.
Small aquatic animals when young; fish, turtles, birds and mammals become important as it grows.
Females guard nests and assist hatchlings. Basking regulates body temperature.
Broad rounded snout, dark armoured body and powerful tail; the large fourth lower tooth is hidden when closed.
Green sea turtle
A marine turtle whose diet shifts as it grows from a young omnivore toward a largely plant-based adult diet.
Oceanic waters during early life, then coastal feeding areas including seagrass beds; eggs are laid on sandy beaches.
Young eat small animals and other floating foods; older turtles largely eat seagrass and algae.
Undertakes movements between feeding and breeding sites. Females dig nests ashore and cover the eggs.
Smooth oval carapace, flipper-like limbs and small head; the name refers to greenish body fat, not a green shell.
Hermann’s tortoise
A Mediterranean land tortoise with a shell that provides shelter and physical protection.
Open woodland, scrub and grassland with sunny patches and hiding places.
Mostly low-growing plants, leaves and flowers; other items may be taken occasionally.
Active by day and hibernates in colder seasons. Females bury eggs in soil.
Domed yellow-and-dark shell, sturdy scaled legs and a small horny tip on the tail; markings vary geographically.
Sand lizard
A sun-loving lizard requiring a mosaic of sheltered vegetation and open ground for reproduction.
Heathland, dunes and other sunny open habitats with cover and suitable sandy nesting ground.
Small invertebrate prey found among low vegetation and exposed ground.
Warms by basking and shelters in vegetation. Females bury eggs in sunny sand; seasonal cold brings hibernation.
Stocky build, patterned brown back with longitudinal lines; breeding males show vivid green flanks.
Komodo dragon
A large monitor lizard that combines predation and scavenging in island ecosystems.
Dry grassland, scrub and woodland on a limited set of Indonesian islands.
Mammals and other vertebrates, with carrion also important; young take smaller prey.
A forked tongue gathers chemical information. Young often climb trees, while large adults are more terrestrial.
Heavy body, long low head, strong claws, rough grey-brown scales and a muscular tapering tail.
Ball python
A non-venomous African constrictor that uses its coils to subdue animal prey.
Savanna grassland and open woodland of western and central Africa; burrows provide shelter.
Small mammals and birds, swallowed whole after capture.
Often active at dusk or night. It may curl into a tight ball defensively; females coil around their eggs.
Heavy body, narrow neck and dark brown blotches enclosing paler patches; captive colour forms vary greatly.
Tuatara
A reptile of the rhynchocephalian lineage, distinct from modern lizards despite its similar outline.
Cool coastal and island habitats in New Zealand, using burrows and sheltered ground.
Invertebrates, eggs and small vertebrates, captured with specialised jaw teeth.
Often solitary and territorial around burrows. Activity can continue at temperatures cool for many other reptiles.
Grey or olive body, spiny crest on neck and back, large head and no external ear opening.
Common frog
A terrestrial frog that returns to freshwater to reproduce and develop as a tadpole.
Damp woodland, grassland and gardens; ponds and shallow waters are used for breeding.
Adults take insects, worms and other invertebrates; tadpoles use different aquatic foods.
Often hides in moist cover by day. Eggs are laid in gelatinous clumps, then larvae metamorphose into froglets.
Variable brown, grey or reddish skin, dark patch behind the eye and long hind limbs.
Common toad
A ground-dwelling amphibian whose breeding migration connects terrestrial feeding areas to ponds.
Woodland, gardens, hedges and rough grassland, with ponds for reproduction.
Slugs, snails and other invertebrates, with larger prey occasionally taken.
Usually walks rather than making long jumps. It hibernates in sheltered places and lays eggs in strings.
Olive-brown warty skin, copper-coloured eyes, short hind legs and conspicuous glands behind the eyes.
Axolotl
An aquatic salamander retaining larval features, including external gills, when sexually mature.
Historically lakes near Mexico City; native remaining habitat is associated with the Xochimilco wetland system.
Small aquatic animals, including worms, molluscs, crustaceans and fish, sucked into the mouth.
Generally solitary and aquatic throughout life under normal conditions. It has notable tissue-regeneration abilities.
Three feathery gill branches on each side of the head and a finned tail; wild animals are usually dark, unlike pale captive forms.
Fire salamander
A forest salamander whose conspicuous colours advertise skin defences.
Shady moist woodland, hiding beneath logs, rocks and in crevices; nearby water supports larvae.
Earthworms, insects, slugs and other available invertebrates.
Often active on mild damp nights. Many populations deposit live larvae into water rather than laying exposed eggs.
Black body with yellow or orange patches and bands, sturdy limbs and a cylindrical tail.
Great white shark
A powerful cartilaginous predator whose senses help locate prey across coastal and offshore habitats.
Temperate and subtropical marine waters, from continental shelves to offshore routes.
Fish and other marine animals; marine mammals become important prey for many larger individuals.
An active swimmer that can travel widely. Behaviour and prey choice vary with size and location.
Grey upper surface, white underside, conical snout, triangular dorsal fin and crescent-shaped tail.
Whale shark
A very large shark that feeds mainly on small organisms filtered from water.
Warm marine waters, often near productive coastal zones but also in offshore waters.
Plankton and small schooling animals gathered by swimming with the mouth open or by suction feeding.
Often solitary, but food-rich sites can attract aggregations. It may feed at the surface or at depth.
Broad flat head, wide terminal mouth and pale spots and stripes over a dark body.
Zebrafish
A small schooling freshwater fish widely studied in developmental biology.
Shallow slow-moving streams, ditches and floodplain waters of southern Asia.
Zooplankton, small aquatic insects and other tiny foods, including insects falling on the surface.
Active by day and forms shoals. Individuals develop dominance relationships during social interactions.
Slender body with dark horizontal stripes running along pale flanks and fine mouth barbels.
Atlantic salmon
A migratory fish whose common life cycle connects freshwater nursery habitat with marine feeding areas.
Cool rivers with gravel spawning beds, followed by marine waters; some populations remain in freshwater.
Young eat aquatic insect larvae; larger marine fish take other fish and crustaceans.
Many adults return to their natal river to spawn, using sensory cues associated with their earlier development.
Streamlined body, small adipose fin and spotted flanks; silvery marine adults change appearance for spawning.
Short-snouted seahorse
A small armoured fish whose male carries developing offspring in a brood pouch.
Shallow sheltered marine waters, including estuaries and vegetation-covered seabeds.
Small live crustaceans captured by rapidly sucking water through the tubular snout.
Anchors itself with a prehensile tail and waits in ambush. Courtship precedes transfer of eggs into the male pouch.
Head angled to a short angular trunk, short upturned snout and curled tail; colour is highly variable.
Common carp
A robust freshwater fish that searches bottom sediments for a mixed diet.
Lakes, reservoirs and rivers, especially slower waters with soft bottom sediments.
Benthic invertebrates, seeds and other plant material; young use planktonic foods.
Often moves in small groups. Feeding disturbs sediment and can influence water clarity.
Deep body, long dorsal fin, protrusible mouth and barbels; domesticated forms differ in scale coverage.
Western honeybee
A eusocial bee with a reproductive queen, workers and males sharing a colony.
Flower-rich meadows, woodland edges and gardens; colonies nest in cavities or managed hives.
Nectar supplies sugars and pollen supplies other nutrients; honey stores help sustain the colony.
Worker tasks change with age. Dance communication helps recruit nestmates to food sources.
Hairy thorax, banded abdomen, two pairs of wings and pollen baskets on worker hind legs.
Buff-tailed bumblebee
A social bumblebee whose colonies often occupy abandoned underground rodent nests.
Gardens, grasslands and other flower-rich habitats with suitable underground nest cavities.
Nectar and pollen from a wide range of flowers; its relatively short tongue limits some tubular flowers.
Queens establish colonies and produce workers, then males and new queens; timing varies with climate.
Hairy black body with two yellow bands. Queens have a buff tail; workers can resemble white-tailed bumblebees closely.
Monarch butterfly
A butterfly whose larvae acquire defensive plant compounds from milkweeds.
Open flower-rich habitats with milkweed host plants; some populations use forested overwintering sites.
Caterpillars eat milkweed leaves; adults drink nectar from flowers.
Some populations undertake long seasonal migrations, while others are more resident.
Orange wings crossed by dark veins, broad dark borders and rows of pale spots.
Red admiral
A strong-flying butterfly whose dark wings are marked by vivid red bands.
Gardens, woodland edges and flower-rich open habitats; nettles provide larval food.
Caterpillars feed mainly on nettles; adults use nectar and also juices from ripe or fallen fruit.
Seasonal movements bring migrants to many areas. Caterpillars shelter within folded leaves.
Dark wings, red bands and white forewing spots; the undersides are more mottled and cryptic.
Seven-spot ladybird
A predatory beetle whose adults and larvae consume aphids in many plant communities.
Grassland, gardens, farmland and woodland margins, usually among low vegetation.
Mostly aphids found on a broad range of host plants, with other foods sometimes used.
Eggs develop into active larvae and then pupae. Adults may gather in sheltered overwintering places.
Red wing covers typically bearing seven dark spots; black thorax with white corner patches. Spots do not indicate age.
Common octopus
A soft-bodied cephalopod with flexible arms, problem-solving abilities and rapid camouflage changes.
Coastal seabeds with rocky crevices and sheltered dens; species identity within the wider complex requires care.
Molluscs and other bottom-dwelling animals captured with arms and handled using a beak.
Often hides in a den. Skin colour, texture and posture change to conceal it on different backgrounds.
Eight sucker-bearing arms, rounded mantle and no external shell; colour is variable rather than fixed.
Common starfish
A seabed echinoderm whose hydraulic tube feet support movement and prey handling.
Rocky and other coastal seabeds of the northeastern Atlantic, including shallow shores.
Often bivalves and other invertebrates; it can extend its stomach into a slightly opened shell.
Moves using many coordinated tube feet. It can turn itself upright through coordinated arm movements.
Usually five tapering arms around a central disc, rough upper surface and orange, brown or purple colour variants.
